paragraphs: Automated data augmentation searches for transformations that help train a model. Many approaches choose from a discrete collection of transformations whose boundaries are designed by hand. This paper investigates how to make that search continuous, so the augmentation system is less constrained by a predefined menu.

The authors construct a mapping from vectors of real numbers to image transformations. They then formulate augmentation design as optimization over the parameters of a distribution in this continuous space. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics provides the mechanism for both learning and sampling augmentations. The mapping potentially gives access to infinitely many transformations, while the continuous formulation opens the problem to gradient-based optimization methods.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report improved efficiency compared with previous methods. The contribution is therefore both a different representation of the search space and a way to explore it. The results support the practical value of continuous augmentation design, while the broader possibility of exploring infinitely many augmentations remains a capability of the formulation.
neurips-2021-a-continuous-mapping-for-au.tldr: A continuous mapping to image transformations enables gradient-based augmentation search and improves efficiency across multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: How should several probability distributions be summarized by one distribution? A conventional Wasserstein barycenter supplies a geometric average. This paper introduces a different summary, called a weak barycenter, whose purpose is to extract geometric information that all the input distributions share.

The construction uses optimal weak transport of mass. The authors analyze its mathematical properties and interpret it through convex ordering, a relationship between probability distributions. Their interpretation represents the shared information as a latent random variable underlying every input distribution. This changes what the summary is meant to capture: common structure across the inputs, rather than their geometric average.

The paper also develops an iterative computation method for a finite collection of distributions and a stochastic method for arbitrary populations of distributions. The latter is particularly suitable when distributions arrive sequentially in a stream. Synthetic examples and two-dimensional real-world data illustrate and validate the approach, with comparisons to standard Wasserstein barycenters showing how the two notions summarize distributions differently.
neurips-2021-a-novel-notion-of-barycente.tldr: Weak barycenters summarize geometric information shared across distributions, with algorithms for finite collections and streaming observations.

paragraphs: Bayesian reinforcement learning represents uncertainty while an agent learns how to act. Existing approaches commonly place that uncertainty over the environment's transitions or its action values. This paper instead studies uncertainty in the Bellman operator, the rule used to update value estimates from rewards and estimates of future value.

The motivating observation concerns bootstrapping: learning updates that depend on other learned estimates. The authors argue that, with bootstrapping, model-free Bayesian methods actually infer a distribution over Bellman operators. Their Bayesian Bellman operator framework makes this interpretation explicit and uses it to analyze how Bayesian methods relate to established frequentist approaches.

The theoretical results establish consistency with frequentist reinforcement learning solutions, including when inference is approximate, and identify conditions supporting convergence. Experiments show that algorithms derived from the framework can explore effectively enough to solve continuous control tasks where the compared regularized actor-critic methods fail severely. These findings connect a revised account of uncertainty to both formal analysis and demonstrated exploration behavior.
neurips-2021-bayesian-bellman-operators-.tldr: Modeling uncertainty in Bellman operators provides theoretical insight into Bayesian reinforcement learning and yields algorithms with strong demonstrated exploration.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial effort communicating between devices. Compression reduces the information sent during each exchange, while accelerated optimization reduces how many exchanges are needed. This paper develops CANITA to combine these two benefits for distributed optimization of general convex objectives.

CANITA builds on the ANITA gradient method and incorporates compressed communication. Its convergence guarantee accounts for the objective's smoothness, the desired error, the number of devices, and the compression parameter. This matters because reducing communication per round is only part of the problem: the overall benefit also depends on how compression affects the number of rounds required.

The authors establish an accelerated rate that improves on the stated nonaccelerated DIANA rate. When there are sufficiently many devices or compression is not too high, CANITA achieves a communication-round dependence proportional to the square root of smoothness divided by target error. Earlier bounds scale directly with that ratio. The result shows that compressed messages and fewer rounds can coexist under the stated conditions.
neurips-2021-canita-faster-rates-for-dis.tldr: CANITA combines communication compression with provable acceleration for distributed convex optimization under conditions on device count and compression.

paragraphs: Highly nonlinear dynamical systems are difficult to model because their behavior can be complex and predictions also need meaningful uncertainty estimates. Methods often depend on techniques tailored to a particular problem. This paper proposes a domain-agnostic approach that combines building blocks derived from ordinary differential equations.

Those building blocks are physics-informed random features, composed to form the model. The architecture uses approximate inference methods developed for deep Gaussian processes. In particular, layer-wise approximations expressed through weights allow random Fourier features to be incorporated, while stochastic variational inference supplies approximate Bayesian inference. Together, these components support a compositional probabilistic model for nonlinear behavior.

Experiments provide evidence that the approach can capture strong nonlinear patterns in real-world time series containing multiple variables. On benchmark regression tasks, it performs comparably to several other probabilistic models. The findings support the usefulness of combining differential-equation-derived features with probabilistic inference, including beyond the dynamical-system examples, without claiming uniformly superior predictive performance.
neurips-2021-compositional-modeling-of-n.tldr: Composed features derived from differential equations enable probabilistic modeling of nonlinear dynamics, with supporting time-series and regression results.

paragraphs: Aligning two sequences means determining which elements correspond, even when the sequences have different lengths or unfold at different speeds. Dynamic Time Warping handles timing shifts and stretching, but unrelated elements scattered through either sequence can undermine the resulting alignment. This paper addresses that problem directly.

Drop-DTW jointly aligns the shared signal and excludes elements treated as outliers. Both decisions are handled within one efficient dynamic program, so dropping elements is part of finding the alignment. The procedure is also fully differentiable, allowing it to serve as a training loss as well as a measure of similarity between sequences.

The experiments demonstrate robustness for sequence retrieval and usefulness across several learning applications. These include locating instructional steps in videos, learning representations from noisy videos, and connecting audio with visual content for retrieval and localization. The reported state-of-the-art results apply to the weakly supervised or unsupervised settings studied. They show how handling unmatched content within alignment can benefit both comparison and representation learning.
neurips-2021-drop-dtw-aligning-common-si.tldr: Drop-DTW aligns shared sequence content while excluding outliers, providing a differentiable similarity measure and training loss.

paragraphs: A molecular graph can correspond to multiple three-dimensional conformations. Predicting this collection matters for molecular modeling and drug discovery. GeoMol tackles the problem by generating distributions of low-energy structures while explicitly modeling local atomic geometry and torsion angles, which describe twisting around bonds.

The model uses message passing neural networks to gather local and global information from the molecular graph. It predicts geometric components with limited redundancy, including one torsion angle per non-terminal bond. These local predictions are sufficient both to compute the training loss and to assemble a full conformer deterministically at test time. The approach is end-to-end, non-autoregressive, and invariant to overall rotations and translations.

An optimal-transport-based loss encourages diversity among generated conformers without adversarial training. The authors report that GeoMol outperforms most of the compared open-source, commercial, and machine learning approaches while delivering substantial speed improvements. The findings support generating molecular ensembles through carefully chosen geometric components, with diversity addressed explicitly during training.
neurips-2021-geomol-torsional-geometric-.tldr: GeoMol generates diverse molecular conformers from local geometry and torsion predictions, predominantly outperforming compared methods with substantial speedups.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes demanding when good decisions depend on consequences far into the future. Learning from scratch can require interactions or computation that grow with this planning horizon. This paper develops a framework for using heuristics drawn from domain knowledge or offline data to accelerate learning.

The framework turns heuristic guidance into a shorter-horizon subproblem and provides a theoretical account of how that subproblem can solve the original task. It also interprets the shortened horizon as a way to regulate the balance between bias and variance when interactions are limited. The analysis characterizes useful heuristics and how their properties affect acceleration.

A central idea is an improvable heuristic, which can let an agent cautiously go beyond what its prior knowledge already supports. The authors apply the framework to accelerate several existing algorithms in simulated robotic control and procedurally generated games. These demonstrations show how prior knowledge can shape the learning problem itself, complementing approaches that use demonstrations or exploratory data to initialize learning.
neurips-2021-heuristic-guided-reinforcem.tldr: Heuristic guidance can shorten reinforcement learning's effective horizon, with theory and experiments showing how suitable prior knowledge accelerates learning.

paragraphs: Partial domain adaptation transfers learning from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain whose classes form a subset of the source classes. Many methods reduce the influence of source examples from classes absent in the target. This paper asks whether those extra classes can still contribute useful visual information.

The proposed method weights information at the feature level. A class2vec module extracts implicit semantic topics from visual features, and an attention layer measures the response to each topic. The method then aligns these semantic responses between source and target data. This creates a way to retain relevant information distributed across multiple categories, including categories that would otherwise be downweighted as whole groups of examples.

Experiments on several cross-domain benchmarks show the method's effectiveness relative to the compared state-of-the-art partial adaptation approaches. Additional analyses examine the semantic alignment mechanism. The contribution is a finer-grained approach to selective transfer: learning which features are relevant when source and target label spaces differ.
neurips-2021-implicit-semantic-response-.tldr: Aligning semantic responses at the feature level helps partial domain adaptation retain useful information from otherwise irrelevant source classes.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes describe a distribution over possible functions. Their kernel controls the kinds of patterns the model tends to expect, and kernel hyperparameters adjust those preferences. A common learning approach selects hyperparameters by optimizing marginal likelihood. This paper studies how to account for uncertainty about those settings in the predictions.

The authors propose using nested sampling to marginalize kernel hyperparameters: predictions incorporate a range of plausible settings instead of relying on one optimized choice. Nested sampling is motivated by its suitability for complex distributions with multiple modes. In this setting, multiple modes correspond to distinct plausible regions of hyperparameter values that uncertainty estimation needs to consider.

The study compares the approach with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on time-series and two-dimensional regression problems. The reported finding is that principled treatment of hyperparameter uncertainty substantially improves prediction intervals. This places the emphasis on how well predictions express uncertainty, and shows why uncertainty about the kernel itself can matter to the final predictive distribution.
neurips-2021-marginalised-gaussian-proce.tldr: Nested sampling integrates Gaussian process kernel uncertainty, with experiments finding substantial improvements in prediction intervals.

paragraphs: Predicting whether two graph nodes should be connected often depends on graph structure, such as shared neighbors, node degrees, and distances. The paper observes that graph neural networks can underperform simple structural heuristics on this task because they rely heavily on smoothed node features. Success on node or graph classification does not automatically resolve that mismatch.

Neo-GNNs address it by learning structural features directly from the adjacency matrix, which records the graph's connections. They estimate overlap between neighborhoods and extend the idea to neighborhoods spanning multiple hops. The architecture also generalizes heuristic methods based on neighborhood overlap, incorporating that useful structural principle into a learned model.

Across the evaluated Open Graph Benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently state-of-the-art link prediction performance. These findings support explicitly representing structural relationships between candidate endpoints. The contribution is particularly relevant to link prediction, where whether two neighborhoods overlap can provide information that feature smoothing alone does not adequately capture.
neurips-2021-neo-gnns-neighborhood-overl.tldr: Neo-GNNs learn neighborhood-overlap structure for link prediction and achieve consistently state-of-the-art results on the evaluated OGB datasets.

paragraphs: A conventional convolutional network sends every input through the same sequence of processing blocks. This paper proposes letting intermediate features determine which specialized block handles them. The aim is to make each block's learning problem easier by directing similar features to the same procedure.

The routing mechanism introduces parallel Procedural Units at each network stage. Each unit contains a processing block and a memory head that summarizes a type of feature. For an incoming intermediate feature, the network finds the closest memory and chooses its corresponding block. This selection operates during both training and testing, allowing the parallel blocks to specialize around the features routed to them.

The authors provide a four-step strategy for efficient training. Experiments show accuracy improvements for VGGNet, ResNet, and EfficientNet on Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet, and CIFAR-100, with negligible additional computation reported. The results support memory-based routing as a way to improve existing architectures through specialization while keeping the extra processing cost small in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-neural-routing-by-memory-b3.tldr: Memory-based routing directs similar intermediate features to specialized convolutional blocks, improving tested networks with negligible extra computation.

paragraphs: Some learning systems contain components defined implicitly, such as an equilibrium or the solution of an optimization problem. Training requires tracking how those solutions change when parameters change. This becomes harder when the underlying functions are nonsmooth, because ordinary derivative formulas may no longer apply.

The paper establishes a nonsmooth implicit function theorem together with calculus rules that can be used in computations. The result applies to definable problems, a broad class covering many practical cases, provided a nonsmooth version of an invertibility condition holds. Within the supported setting, substituting Clarke Jacobians for ordinary derivatives in familiar formulas is mathematically justified and compatible with backpropagation.

Applications include deep equilibrium networks, neural networks containing conic optimization layers, and hyperparameter tuning for nonsmooth Lasso-type models. Numerical experiments also demonstrate highly pathological gradient behavior when implicit differentiation is applied without appropriate hypotheses. These examples explain why the assumptions matter: the paper supplies conditions under which a convenient differentiation procedure has a sound mathematical foundation.
neurips-2021-nonsmooth-implicit-differen.tldr: A nonsmooth implicit function theorem justifies backpropagation-compatible differentiation rules under definability and generalized invertibility conditions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from existing data. Actor-critic methods are widely used for this purpose, but their theoretical foundations are less developed than their practical adoption. This paper proposes an offline actor-critic algorithm that incorporates pessimism and establishes guarantees for the policy it returns.

The algorithm operates under a closure condition on the Bellman evaluation operator for the action-value functions associated with the actor's policies. This setting is more general than the low-rank Markov decision process model. Despite that broader scope, the procedure remains computationally tractable through a sequence of second-order programs, linking the theoretical construction to an explicit optimization procedure.

The performance bound depends on how well the available data cover a comparator policy. That comparator can be arbitrary and may itself depend on the data, making the guarantee flexible about the policy used for comparison. A minimax lower bound matches the achievable guarantee up to logarithmic factors, indicating that the analysis captures the fundamental difficulty of the studied setting closely.
neurips-2021-provable-benefits-of-actor-.tldr: A pessimistic offline actor-critic algorithm provides tractable optimization and nearly matching performance bounds tied to comparator-policy data coverage.

paragraphs: An online reinforcement learning agent may be unable to update its behavior after every new observation. This paper studies two such restrictions: learning in batches and changing policies only rarely. The setting is episodic linear Markov decision processes, where rewards and transition probabilities have linear representations using known features.

The authors develop a separate algorithm for each restriction. For batch learning, their bound shows that roughly the square root of T divided by dH batches suffices to match the stated regret rate of LSVI-UCB, up to logarithmic factors. Here T counts interactions, d is feature dimension, and H is episode length. For rare policy switching, roughly dH log T switches suffice for that same rate.

These are sufficiency results: they establish that strong regret guarantees remain achievable with substantially less adaptation. A lower bound for batch learning additionally suggests that the batch-count dependence in the proposed upper bound is tight. Together, the results quantify how restricting updates affects learning under the paper's linear-model assumptions.
neurips-2021-provably-efficient-reinforc.tldr: For episodic linear decision processes, two algorithms match LSVI-UCB's regret rate using substantially fewer batches or policy changes.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves one optimization problem whose outcome affects another, as in hyperparameter optimization and meta-learning. Faster algorithms are valuable because solving these coupled problems can be computationally demanding. This paper targets a gap between momentum methods proposed for speed and the computational improvements that had actually been proved.

The authors introduce two algorithms. One uses recursive iterations with momentum. The other uses recursive gradient estimates within nested loops to reduce variance. Both achieve a stated computational complexity proportional to the target accuracy raised to minus 1.5, ignoring logarithmic factors. The previous SGD-based bound scales with accuracy raised to minus 2, and the earlier momentum methods had not provably improved it.

The smaller exponent means that the theoretical cost grows more slowly as the requested error tolerance becomes tighter. Experiments in hyperparameter optimization support the theoretical findings and show improved empirical performance. The contribution therefore combines new recursive optimization procedures with a stronger complexity guarantee and practical evidence in an application of bilevel learning.
neurips-2021-provably-faster-algorithms-.tldr: Two recursive bilevel optimization algorithms improve the stated complexity exponent from 2 to 1.5, with supporting hyperparameter-optimization experiments.

paragraphs: A DNA fragment has two complementary strands, so sequencing it can produce either of two reverse-complement representations of the same fragment. Machine learning models can use this symmetry to make learning easier. Reverse-complement equivariance means that transforming the input in this way produces a corresponding, predictable transformation inside the model.

Earlier work had introduced particular convolutional architectures with this property, but the broader range of possible designs was unclear. This paper characterizes all linear reverse-complement-equivariant layers and establishes that additional architectures exist. It also discusses compatible pointwise nonlinearities, which are needed to turn linear layers into richer neural networks while preserving the symmetry.

The authors further examine equivariant embeddings of k-mers, short nucleotide sequences, as an alternative to encoding individual nucleotides with one-hot vectors. Experiments show that the new architectures can outperform existing ones. The contribution expands the mathematical design space for DNA models and provides evidence that exploring that larger space can yield practical improvements.
neurips-2021-reverse-complement-equivari.tldr: Characterizing all linear reverse-complement-equivariant layers reveals new DNA network architectures that can outperform existing designs.

paragraphs: Smoothed online learning charges a learner both for its current decision and for changing that decision over time. The paper studies how to balance these hitting and switching costs under two performance measures. A crucial distinction is whether the learner sees the current hitting cost before acting.

When that cost is available, the authors analyze competitive ratios under specified growth conditions. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone improves existing guarantees for polyhedral functions and functions with quadratic growth. When convexity and quadratic growth both hold, minimizing a weighted combination of hitting and switching costs gives a stronger guarantee.

When the convex hitting cost is hidden until after prediction, the paper modifies Ader to account for switching costs. Smoothed Ader achieves an optimal dynamic-regret bound scaling as the square root of T times one plus comparator path length. This path length measures how much the comparison sequence moves. If costs are revealed beforehand, a similar guarantee holds without bounded gradients, with a matching lower bound confirming optimality.
neurips-2021-revisiting-smoothed-online-.tldr: Simple cost-balancing strategies and Smoothed Ader improve guarantees for online learning with switching costs under distinct information and growth assumptions.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning usually requires constraints to be written mathematically, which can demand specialized expertise. This paper studies whether an agent can instead learn to interpret constraints expressed in ordinary language. The goal is to pursue rewards while respecting instructions about forbidden situations.

The authors introduce HAZARDWORLD, a multitask benchmark with free-form textual constraints. Their agent separates interpretation from policy learning. A constraint interpreter translates text into spatial and temporal representations of forbidden states. A policy network then uses those representations to learn behavior that minimizes constraint violations during training, including while learning new tasks.

Across the evaluated HAZARDWORLD domains, the method achieves rewards up to eleven times higher and fewer violations by a factor of 1.8 compared with existing approaches. These are comparative improvements, rather than a guarantee of violation-free behavior. The authors also report that absolute performance remains challenging: agents still struggle to learn efficiently in the benchmark. The work establishes a concrete setting and architecture for studying language-specified constraints.
neurips-2021-safe-reinforcement-learning.tldr: A modular agent interprets textual constraints and improves rewards and constraint adherence on HAZARDWORLD, though efficient learning remains challenging.

paragraphs: Multi-object tracking requires maintaining separate object identities through a video. This paper trains a recurrent tracking model using unlabeled video. The authors identify a problem with earlier self-supervision signals: they can produce degenerate recurrent models that follow shortcuts, such as matching detections according to proximity to the initial detections.

The proposed training signal is cross-input consistency. For the same video sequence, the method creates two inputs that hide different information. A recurrent model independently produces tracks from each input, and training encourages the resulting tracks to agree. Agreement across these differently obscured inputs supplies supervision without requiring labeled tracks.

Evaluations on MOT17 and KITTI show that the approach outperforms four named supervised methods: Tracktor++, FAMNet, GSM, and mmMOT. This demonstrates that the proposed self-supervision can support competitive tracking despite training only on unlabeled video. The central contribution is the design of a consistency requirement suited to recurrent multi-object tracking, where previously proposed signals were found to encourage unhelpful solutions.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-multi-objec.tldr: Cross-input consistency trains recurrent multi-object trackers on unlabeled video and outperforms four supervised methods in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Determining a causal direction from observational data involves two different questions: whether the direction is identifiable in principle, and whether a statistical procedure can reach it while controlling errors at every sample size. This paper separates those questions for linear, acyclic causal models with non-Gaussian noise and hidden confounding variables.

Without latent confounders, earlier results establish statistical decidability: a method can converge to the correct orientation while keeping its probability of an incorrect orientation below any specified positive tolerance at every sample size. With latent confounders and faithfulness, prior work still identifies orientations among observed variables, although the full causal model need not be uniquely identified.

The paper shows that this remaining identifiability does not preserve statistical decidability. Convergence to the correct orientation is possible, but it cannot be paired with the specified finite-sample error guarantees, even under faithfulness. This clarifies a gap between eventual correctness and controlled errors along the way. The authors also suggest model adjustments that may restore decidability.
neurips-2021-statistical-undecidability-.tldr: Latent confounders can preserve causal-orientation identifiability while making convergence with uniformly controlled finite-sample orientation errors impossible.

paragraphs: Video recognition depends on summarizing a sequence into a useful representation. Simple global averaging can miss complex dynamics, while ordinary covariance pooling ignores the ordering needed to describe video structure. This paper introduces Temporal-attentive Covariance Pooling, or TCP, to summarize relationships within and across frames.

TCP first applies temporal attention to adjust spatial and temporal features before covariance pooling. It then pools attentive covariance representations to capture both correlations within frames and cross-correlations between frames. A fast matrix power normalization uses the geometry of the resulting covariance representation. Together, these operations aim to preserve richer temporal information in the final video summary.

The module is designed to fit at the end of different video architectures. Experiments across six benchmarks, including Kinetics, Something-Something V1, and Charades, show improvements over the corresponding architectures and report strong generalization. The findings support improving video recognition through the way features are aggregated, with attention and covariance jointly contributing to a representation of temporal dynamics.
neurips-2021-temporal-attentive-covarian.tldr: Temporal-attentive covariance pooling captures within-frame and between-frame relationships, improving video recognition across six evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Several parties may want to combine their predictive expertise while keeping labeled data and model parameters to themselves. This paper proposes a decentralized mechanism for making collective predictions at test time. It uses existing trained models without requiring pooled data, retraining, or an external validation set.

Inspired by human consensus-making, the method exchanges information through queries among agents. Its theoretical analysis shows that, in the large-sample limit, the procedure recovers inverse mean-squared-error weighting. That weighting is optimal for combining independent, unbiased estimators, so the interpretation depends on those qualifications and on the limiting setting.

Experiments show that the mechanism combines models whose quality varies across the input space. The resulting consensus improves over classical model averaging and even over evaluated weighted schemes with access to additional validation data. A decentralized Jackknife procedure also measures how sensitive the collective prediction is to one agent's contribution. Together, the methods address both forming a shared prediction and assessing an individual participant's influence on it.
neurips-2021-test-time-collective-predic.tldr: A decentralized consensus mechanism combines pretrained models at test time and improves over evaluated averaging methods without external validation data.

paragraphs: Decision trees classify examples through a sequence of branching decisions and are popular for their lightweight, interpretable operation. This paper introduces Tree in Tree, or TnT, which expands that structure into a directed acyclic decision graph. The aim is to obtain stronger classifiers while using smaller models.

TnT constructs its graph by recursively growing decision trees inside internal nodes or leaf nodes. This gives the construction a richer building block than a single greedy decision at each step. The reported time complexity grows linearly with the number of nodes in the resulting graph, supporting the use of the method on large datasets.

The authors show improved classification performance and reduced model size compared with decision trees. These benefits appear both when TnT is used as an individual classifier and when it supplies the base estimators in bagging or AdaBoost ensembles. The findings suggest that changing the structure and construction of a tree-based classifier can improve both predictive performance and model compactness.
neurips-2021-tree-in-tree-from-decision-.tldr: Tree in Tree recursively builds decision graphs that improve classification performance while using smaller models than the compared decision trees.

paragraphs: Ensemble-based debiasing uses a model focused on dataset bias to adjust the learning target of another classifier. The intended effect is to reduce dependence on that bias. This paper examines an often overlooked part of the process: whether the bias-only model accurately expresses uncertainty about its predictions.

The authors prove that inaccurate uncertainty estimates from the bias-only model can damage debiasing performance. They also find empirically that existing bias-only models do not estimate uncertainty accurately enough. These results identify confidence quality as consequential to the correction process, because the bias model's outputs help determine how the main classifier is trained.

The proposed solution adds calibration between bias modeling and debiasing, creating a three-stage pipeline. Experiments on natural language inference and fact verification show consistently higher out-of-distribution accuracy than the traditional two-stage approach. The findings support treating calibration of the auxiliary bias model as part of debiasing itself, since errors in its uncertainty can affect the final classifier's ability to generalize.
neurips-2021-uncertainty-calibration-for.tldr: Calibrating the bias-only model improves ensemble-based debiasing, yielding consistently better out-of-distribution accuracy in the evaluated language tasks.
